title: Wildfires: Are We Ready for Next Summer?
label: 15 Sep 2026 · Wildfire readiness
summary: This hearing looked at how the UK handled a record-breaking wildfire season, with over 1,300 fires and homes destroyed. Two government departments — one in charge of fire services, one in charge of the environment and farming — were asked about prevention, water supply, alerts, planning rules and whether enough money and coordination are in place. Ministers and officials admitted the current system isn't fit for the future, promised action before next spring, but couldn't give firm timelines or budgets for many measures.

chapters.title: A record-breaking fire season
chapters.takeaway: Both ministers admitted the summer's wildfires were unprecedented and that current plans are not fit for the future.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This summer was dreadful for wildfires — record numbers, 19 homes destroyed, over 50,000 acres burned. What lessons has the Government learned?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We've come out of this summer in a very different place. We had over 1,300 wildfires — record numbers. What we have in place now isn't going to manage fires in 10 years' time. We need to look again at land management, how we respond, and how people behave.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The response from the fire service was extraordinary. One big lesson for me is that fire and wildfires are in the right place back in our department. The real change is that fires are now hitting the edges of towns and threatening homes and vital infrastructure, not just rural areas. We need to focus on preventing fires, not just fighting them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Rural communities have lived with this for years. Is it going to take homes burning in places like Stourbridge for the Government to take this seriously?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I agree. The public now sees the risk in a way they maybe didn't before. But the impact has been profound for rural people for many years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Fires blazed for weeks. It was only when they hit the suburbs that the Prime Minister called a Cobra meeting — that's the Government's emergency committee — and you were appointed. From 22 July to 14 August there was no fire minister at all. What does that say about priority?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Timing is everything. There was a change of Administration and new appointments were being made. The Prime Minister is committed to holding a wildfire summit in October, bringing everyone together.

chapters.title: Coordination across the UK
chapters.takeaway: Everyone agrees fires don't respect borders, but there's no UK-wide strategy yet and the fire minister hasn't spoken to her counterparts in Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This is a national issue now. Do we need a more coordinated UK-wide approach?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The situation in south Wales showed how important it is to work across borders. We need to share resources and anticipate what's coming, just like we look at experience abroad.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have you spoken to your opposite numbers in the devolved administrations?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I have not up to now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Wouldn't that be urgent if you're going to have a UK-wide approach?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Exactly. The Welsh Administration is organising its own summit. We need better coordination at a political level, but work on the ground is happening between administrations.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Fires don't respect borders, so of course we need a joined-up approach — sharing evidence and best practice. Within DEFRA we're already scaling up resources for wildfires. We're working on an action plan now. But we won't fight fires from Whitehall alone; we need to invest in resources on the ground with MHCLG, landowners and land managers.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Have you reached out directly to the Welsh Government and been rebuffed?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We regularly engage with our counterparts in the Welsh, Scottish and Northern Irish Governments.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So why is there no national summit, and why does it look disjointed between Wales and England?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: You'd have to ask the Welsh Government. But I've never had any rebuff from our counterparts. We all agree we need to work across the administrations. My team and I were in Scotland three weeks ago talking to the Scottish Fire Service and Scottish Government.

chapters.title: Fire service capacity and aerial support
chapters.takeaway: Local fire services were stretched to the limit, and the UK relies on ad-hoc commercial deals for firefighting planes — something ministers admit must be fixed before next summer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: My constituency was badly affected. The Chief Fire Officer of Staffordshire said this summer was unprecedented in his 30-year career. Even with extra resources, there were times they were so stretched they didn't have enough fire engines — if another incident happened, they'd have struggled to attend. Do you accept this summer exposed major gaps?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Absolutely. The changing pattern of wildfires throws up issues about how we allocate resources. This summer was unprecedented. We must look carefully at the evidence and prepare better. We have pilots looking at appropriate equipment because traditional methods aren't always right.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The UK doesn't have its own firefighting planes. Any aerial support depends on individual fire services making deals with commercial providers. Isn't that insufficient?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: You're right to raise this. The Prime Minister has committed to considering it at the summit. Fire chiefs told me aerial support is good at putting out flames but not so good at dealing with the underlying fire in heathland. It's right at the top of the agenda.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We've always relied on fire services resourcing themselves, with a thin layer of national assets. That didn't include aerial assets like other countries have. We did deploy some to Manchester, Derbyshire and the Cairngorms, but individual fire services looking for commercial arrangements mid-response isn't going to cut it. We want cost-effective on-call availability in place for next summer — 44 services competing for the same asset isn't cost-effective. We're also looking at drones, including water-carrying drones. We need to solve this for next summer and for the future.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Have you discussed with the Prime Minister whether firefighting planes would be a national asset and how soon they'd be available?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: It's premature to talk about that. I look forward to an in-depth conversation with the Prime Minister at the appropriate time.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We've started conversations with providers. We're not waiting for the summit. We need to work out the mechanism for contracting and allocating — when there are competing needs, someone has to decide the highest operational need. By next summer we need to be in a much better place than this summer.

chapters.title: Strategy, prevention and land management
chapters.takeaway: There's still no national wildfire strategy for England, and the Government is relying on peatland restoration and flexible licensing rather than banning controlled burning — a fight the committee isn't convinced by.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: We've had severe seasons two years running. Why does England still not have a national wildfire strategy, and will you publish one before next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I have a one, two and 10-year vision. The immediate focus is making sure we're in a far stronger place by spring next year. We've increased staff in DEFRA focused on wildfires. We'll go from the action plan into the summit, gather evidence, and make it public. The wider question is how we make ourselves better resourced in the short, medium and longer term.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're working towards a strategy through the action plan, but we're not waiting for that to start coordinating. We have joint governance arrangements between our two departments. That level of coordination across Government hasn't been there. We need to use this as a catalyst and build on pilots through local resilience forums. Weather patterns are unpredictable, so preparedness is critical.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: There's no wildfire management plan in my area. People point to the Cairngorms as an example of an integrated plan. Are you coordinating at a national landscape level?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Local authorities should be developing their own fire resilience plans tailored to their area. DEFRA gives advice on wildfire management, but the evidence about the threat has changed. At Dunwich Heath, what was agreed three years ago — fire breaks wide enough — turned out not to be sufficient. Now they're working with the fire service to widen fire breaks. Advice is changing in light of increased risk.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Local government is central. Local resilience forums should cover every area and bring partnerships together. Every forum needs expertise on wildfires. We're also looking at making wildfire risk explicit in planning policy. We have experience with flooding to learn from. Local authorities are often left to deal with the consequences after a disaster. We need consistency in what every resilience forum should be dealing with.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Some local authorities are run by people who deny climate change, so some things will have to happen nationally. What do you want out of the summit, and how will you make sure all affected parts of the country are represented?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The Prime Minister wants the summit to be about action, not just conversation. It's about sharing best practice, looking at the hard implications and how they affect policy. We need coordination between nations. Fires don't respect boundaries. The summer showed we need to share resources and respond to need across the country.

chapters.title: International lessons and fuel load
chapters.takeaway: The UK is learning from Australia and Europe on behaviour change and tactics, but the committee and ministers clash over whether controlled burning should play a bigger role in reducing fire fuel.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Countries like Australia and EU nations put far more emphasis on prevention and landscape management. Are you doing enough?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We're alive to international lessons. Australia, Canada and Europe have dealt with this for decades. Much of their focus is on behaviour change — heightened awareness during fire season. In my constituency people wanted disposable barbecues banned because they felt the fear. On land management, we have to manage our land appropriately. Peatland restoration is a huge opportunity — it's good for carbon capture and water management, and a wetter moor is a better moor. But it will take time. A lot of the debate focuses on heather and grassland, which covers 5% of the UK but dominates 95% of the debate. Different lands need different management.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Learning from partners is already having an impact. Firefighters in our national wildfire capability trained in South Africa and Poland and brought in tactics like tactical burning. We hosted the World Fire Congress in London last week. We're at the forefront of that international community.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Government has said it's exploring cooperation with the EU's civil protection mechanism. Is that being considered?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The UK can already seek access to EU assets if needed. But over the summer Spain and France needed them more. Their fires were much more significant. We have an MOU with Greece — we're learning from them on wildfire fighting, and helping them on high-rise building fires. But realistically, southern Europe's needs will exceed ours, so we must get our own house in order.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On fuel load — re-wetting is a massive task that takes decades. What is DEFRA doing to reduce fire load on the hills for next year?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Cutting is available. Over the last year we've had 24 applications for burning licences. Two were granted where cutting wasn't accessible. Where cutting can't reach, licences would be approved.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is that over any peat depth?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: The licensing scheme operates where peat depth is greater than 30 cm. There isn't a complete ban on burning. We've had 24 applications, but most weren't for wildfire mitigation — they were for training. We take advice from the Fire and Rescue Service. Their steer is that there are less risky places to train than deep peat.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You expanded the area subject to licensing threefold in 2025. Is that helping get fire load off the hill?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: If your long-term objective is re-wetting, cool burning messes with the hydrology. You have to manage your way through this. We enable people to apply for licences. We haven't had many credible applications. If we get credible ones, we'll issue them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have you heard contrary views from land managers and gamekeepers who end up fighting fires and coughing up ash? Do you respect those views?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: Of course we respect those views. We're continuing to talk to land managers about making the licensing scheme more flexible, but our long-term ambition remains a wetter peatland environment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are you doing to take fire load off the hill before the next fire season?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: That's why we have a licensing scheme, and there are other options like cutting. Those options are there for people to develop wildfire management strategies.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Evidence says the licensing is complex, slow and impractical.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The CLA gave evidence about practicalities — the licence is prescriptive on geolocation, and by the time it's approved the wind or locality might have shifted. We're listening to sensible feedback. It should be a reiterative conversation.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You're funding £2.5 million of research into land management interventions, yet you didn't wait for that evidence before changing the licensing rules. Doesn't that alarm you?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: You never have a perfect evidence base. It's normal for Government to keep investing in improved evidence. We ran a consultation and talked to the National Fire Chiefs Council before making changes. For individual licences, we take advice from the local fire service and Natural England.

chapters.title: The emergency alert, risk register and planning
chapters.takeaway: The nationwide phone alert worked but needs refining, the national risk register underestimates wildfire risk, and planning rules need to catch up with the new reality.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The national emergency alert went out on 14 August. Fires had been burning for weeks. Should it have been issued sooner?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: There are different views. On balance, the benefit was recognised. There needs to be a sophisticated set of procedures for when it's essential. We know it caught the public's attention. There were criticisms about vulnerable people and about the Welsh language version going out before the English one. We'll learn from it and use it judiciously so people don't become complacent.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Was it a success? Has evaluation been done?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Analysis is ongoing, but initial thinking is yes, it raised the importance of the situation. Most fires relate to human activity, so influencing behaviour is key.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The decision was taken at Cobra on the advice of the fire service — not ministers or civil servants. On whether it was a success: the fire service requested it, and it brought public awareness of the risks. Yes, but we need to learn more. The reason some people got six alerts is poor signal — the system keeps trying until it registers. That's a real issue in rural areas.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Who ultimately gave the go-ahead?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: All alerts are ultimately issued by the Cabinet Office. It holds the technology and makes the final decision.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The national risk register — which assesses threats — rates a worst-case wildfire as remote, around 1%, less likely than a volcanic eruption. But we've seen significant wildfires in 2022, 2025 and 2026. Is that assessment accurate?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The risk assessment is held by MHCLG. On whether it's fair, all evidence shows realities have shifted. We're preparing for increased risk because of climate change, drought and the impact on national security.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: There's a review cycle led by the Cabinet Office. We knew the risk was changing, but the speed has been significant. We need to review the risk assessment. On the day the alert went off we had 11 major incidents relating to wildfires across the UK — unprecedented. Wildfires are now more likely than earthquakes.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: When will the risk register be updated?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We'll start that conversation with the Cabinet Office. We haven't done it over the summer because we were dealing with the actual risk. I'd assure you it will be before the next wildfire season. Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On planning — the 2026 national planning policy framework mentions wildfire risk. What role did fire services have in shaping it?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: That was before my time, so I can't give you a false account. I believe fire services were involved via the National Fire Chiefs Council. I can provide details subsequently.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What do you think it means in practice for new developments near wildfire risk?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Basic measures — a fire break to stop fire spreading from rural to urban, and slowing the spread between houses. If you slow it down, you give the fire service time to arrive. Without that, fire can spread so fast they can't get there quickly enough.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is the Chartered Institute of Housing guidance going to be put on a statutory footing?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I can't answer that at the moment. A lot of planning policy works around guidance.

chapters.title: Water, farmers and local response
chapters.takeaway: Water supply during fires is a growing problem, farmers want to build reservoirs but face barriers, and there's no nationwide ban on disposable barbecues — which the committee says sends the wrong signal.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The National Fire Chiefs Council says water availability is a growing challenge. During the New Forest fires, maintaining water supply was an additional challenge. Are you considering stronger requirements on water companies?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I don't have an answer on that specific point right now. We're gathering evidence around supply. I'll take it away.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Regulation of water companies sits with DEFRA. Water companies are represented on local resilience forums. Fire services have contingency plans for water supply, but we've heard it can be an issue. It's something to take between the two of us.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: After the Cobra meeting in August, a drought working group was set up, chaired by Minister Emma Hardy. Water companies, extraction groups, the Environment Agency and farming groups are on those calls. Drought and wildfire season sit side by side.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Professor Emma Howard Boyd told the Committee that during the Wennington 2022 fire, water pressure had been reduced by the water company. There was a delay of hours before pressure was restored. What responsibility should water companies have?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I wasn't aware of that previously. The principle is we need water resilience — holding enough water and making sure companies invest in infrastructure. Measures over the summer, like temporary use bans, helped build resilience.

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: DEFRA works closely with the Environment Agency and water companies on drought planning. There's a legal duty for water companies to maintain emergency preparedness. We'll take this away and look at it properly.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Farmers are often on the frontline. The £15 million for on-farm reservoirs is welcome, but will you tackle planning barriers delaying these?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The £15 million comes with a commitment to unlock barriers, working with MHCLG on planning. There are grants through Farming in Protected Landscapes. In Dorset, farmers are working with their fire service to adapt water tanks. We need to support these smaller adaptations too.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're working with the National Farmers' Union on an evidence-led review around introducing permitted development rights for on-farm reservoirs — that would give farmers more control.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should land managers be able to create wildfire ponds through permitted development rights too?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I'm pleased you've raised it. It will be given full consideration. It feeds into how these things could be managed practically on the ground.

chapters.title: Final push on urgency
chapters.takeaway: The committee pressed for firm deadlines, budgets and a nationwide ban on disposable barbecues, warning that government machinery grinds slowly and next fire season is just months away.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: There's a huge issue with farming profitability and water. Farmers are turning to solar farms and battery storage. The landscape and risk profile are changing. Are we doing enough through planning policy to account for that increased wildfire risk?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: If there are significant changes, they need to be looked at in the context of increased risk. I have Peter here for the technical answer.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: At the World Fire Congress last week, lithium-ion battery storage was the issue being talked about across the world. Fire services are catching up with that risk. We'll always balance enabling development with protecting lives.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: I hope you take that away. If policy doesn't catch up, we'll have permissions granted for significant solar farms with changed risk not accounted for.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On the emergency alert — it was designed for immediate threat to life. If we use it to tell people not to have a barbecue, there's a risk it becomes the boy who cried wolf. Should it be used more locally?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The advice came from the fire service based on evidence I didn't see. Could stuff be tailored if some areas are at higher risk? That should be considered. It wasn't a political or civil servant decision.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Cabinet Office makes the final decision. Does it ever refuse requests?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: You might ask the Cabinet Office to come back to the Committee on that. I don't want to mislead you.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: In Wales, people who don't speak Welsh got an alert they couldn't understand, then waited a significant time for the English version. Has that been fed back?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: It's been fed back to us extremely clearly. It's a broader issue than wildfires. That's been picked up in the lessons learned.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On devolution — local authorities can create by-laws banning disposable barbecues, but they can't enforce on private land. What's your strategy for consistency?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: That relates to the Department for Business and Trade. It's a wider conversation. I still need evidence on how effective the announcement was — some shops still had them for sale after the ban. It's complicated.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Public Spaces Protection Orders can only be used on public land. We need to ensure locally they have the powers to deal with ignition sources, and that they can enforce. That's something we're thinking about.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: I was urging supermarkets to stop selling disposable barbecues. One fire outside my constituency was directly linked to one. The reason businesses flouted the Prime Minister's request is because it was voluntary guidance, not enforceable. Will you take back the need to consider a nationwide ban?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: All things are on the table. But there's also a need for public awareness. Leaving a bottle or litter can be just as dangerous. It goes back to behaviour change and real understanding of the risk. If some people continue anti-social behaviour, responsible community members will step in.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The evidence we got was that when gamekeepers and farmers approach people lighting fires or using barbecues, they get abuse and sometimes threats. A Government signal here would be very important.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I recognise that from farmers around Yorkshire. It must be disheartening to warn people and be ignored, then see the consequences.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Mr Perkins?

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Climate adaptation has been the less fashionable cousin of climate mitigation. The Climate Change Committee described the previous national adaptation plan as not fit for purpose. Do you share that?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: That's prior to my time. We leave this summer in a very different place. The focus must be on making sure the adaptations following the Climate Change Committee's fourth risk assessment, which we'll respond to in January, meet the risks now. I take that evidence seriously.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Climate Change Committee says this Government's work has made no progress. Can we expect a radically different plan 4?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: In adaptation 4 we'll set stronger objectives, preparing for at least 2% warming by 2050 in line with the Climate Change Committee. We're going bolder. But we're not sitting on our hands — we'll do things before it launches, including the wildfire summit.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Why wait until 2028 for plan 4? And will wildlife resilience be recognised as a public good under the farm payment scheme ELMs?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: There are already schemes where farmers can access funding for fire resilience. The task is better awareness. I've asked what more we can do to encourage applications. I don't want farmers out of pocket for doing the right thing.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Why should homeowners at risk be confident the Government will be better prepared by next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I've asked officials to look at one, two and 10-year planning. We must be in a better place by spring next year. There are measures — water storage, water capture, access to ELM programmes. Flooding is a good example: 15 years ago we weren't prepared, now we've come a long way. That's the blueprint for wildfire. We need to use nature and adaptation in that response.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Do you have the budget to do this? DEFRA has been much more stretched than other departments.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: There's lots of money not being taken up through ELM programmes. We need to get it out to people who should be using it. When we come up with plans for future resilience, it must be evidence-led — that allows a conversation rather than saying we need £1 billion without knowing what for. There will be questions about funding, but also about behaviour change — that's not about infrastructure resourcing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've covered the ground we wanted. It's good to see both departments here together — I hope it reflects a future intention for better integration. I'll leave you with one final thought: a greater sense of urgency. It's September. We'll be into the next wildfire season before we know it, and government machinery grinds slowly. It's your jobs, Jenny and Judith, to make sure it doesn't.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I want to go back to the impact on firefighters and communities. We're looking very carefully at the health and wellbeing needs of firefighters. It's critical that we look after the people who keep us safe.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I agree: it's all about the people. That's a good ending point. Thank you for your attendance and engagement.
